title: When the heart is heavy
hookLine: a prophet who grieved out loud, a du'a against worry and grief, and help that isn't a lack of faith

cards: An old man has wept so long over a lost son that his eyes have gone white. His other sons warn him he'll ruin his health, or die of it. He's a prophet: Ya'qub, Jacob, whose story you met in camp two.
And he doesn't stop grieving, or pretend he's fine. He answers, in Pickthall's words: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” A prophet, carrying something heavy, and saying so.

teach.b: The Qur'an and the hadith don't treat sadness as a failure of faith. When the Prophet's ﷺ baby son Ibrahim was dying, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears. A companion was surprised.
The Prophet said, in Bukhari: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Grief and faith, in the same breath. He also taught a du'a for exactly this weight.
Anas, who served him for years, said in Bukhari that he often heard him say: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan.
O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and from grief. Hamm is the weight of what might happen. Hazan is the ache of what already did.
The du'a goes on through helplessness, laziness and the burden of debt: a list of very ordinary heaviness, said often. And he didn't make prayer the only medicine.

teach.h: SEEK TREATMENT: THERE IS A REMEDY.
teach.b: Abu Dawud reports him telling people: seek treatment, servants of Allah, for Allah has not made a disease without making a remedy for it.
Many Muslim scholars and counselors today apply that to the mind as well as the body: therapy and medicine alongside the du'a, not instead of it. Seeing a counselor is using the means Allah provides.

teach.h: IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.
teach.b: So, said plainly: if the heaviness is more than a hard week, if it's taking your sleep or your hope, or if you've thought about not being here, please reach for help today.
In the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help. Tell someone you trust. Ya'qub took his grief to Allah, and he still said it out loud.

how: Many Muslims say the Prophet's du'a against worry and grief in hard times, and many imams and Muslim counselors encourage therapy or medical care alongside prayer.

games.q: Ya'qub's sons warn him that his grief will make him ill. what does he answer?
o: you're right; I'll stop thinking of him.
I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.
grief means my faith is weak.
games.why: he keeps grieving, and takes it to Allah, out loud (12:86). a prophet, carrying something heavy.

practice: Sit comfortably, let your shoulders drop, and name, silently, the heaviest thing you're carrying today, just its name. As you breathe out, picture setting it down in front of you: not gone, just put down for a minute.
If you pray, you can say the du'a, in Arabic or English: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and from grief; if you don't, let each breath out be a little longer than the breath in.

wordCard.voice: Hamm. Worry, the weight of what might happen; in the Prophet's du'a it sits beside hazan, grief. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: worry and grief, from the Prophet's du'a: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan.

carryVoice: Your line: the du'a and the doctor. Both are ways of asking for help, and you're allowed both. Go gently.
